With 276 hours on record at the time of review, I still don't feel 100% qualified to comment on every aspect of the game because it's so massive. I also have every DLC, so your experience might be different without those.

That said, this is the sort of game that you can turn into a second job if you're not careful. It supports a wide variety of playstyles from the casual Han Solo style FPS pilot, to RPG-style completing quests and storylines, to grand empire building and complex industrial/trade styles. And if one gets a bit stale, you can easily dip your toes in another.

If you love Kenshi and want a space version, this is it. It's not the same game, but it has the same vibe. If you love the grand promise of Star Citizen but are frustrated with the current shallow state, this will fill the void. If you want a singleplayer Eve that you can pause and walk away from, this is it. If you grew up loving Elite on the C64 (like I did), this is its spiritual successor. Bannerlord with spaceships? Yep.

The visuals are ok (I suggest desaturating in the options to turn down the gaudy colours) and performance is pretty good on older systems. The developers are very active and mod support is excellent with both Workshop and Nexus thriving. It's not great for streamers as it can be quite a slow burn, but it's largely bug-free and most frustrations are down to player ignorance or can easily be fixed with the right mods. Replayability is high with different starts, dynamic generation and such.

It's not for everyone, but fans of sandboxes will find many things to like about X4.

In my opinion, the X series may be the best single-player 3d space games out there. All of them have a large mostly-hand-made area to explore (if you want pure exploration, I suggest Elite: dangerous or No Man's Sky, which are infinite - but also procedural, while X has always had the areas hand-made, though the buildings aren't), a vast economy to trade with and eventually shape, and a huge array of ships and equipment to choose from. And X4 lives up to that in spades, adding the ability to change the political landscape of the universe by supporting and opposing the various factions (including your own, eventually), ship and equipment mods, and more customization of buildings.

And X4 is really good at letting you do your thing. Want to be a fighter, killing the various threats in the universe? Xenon, Kha'ak, and several pirate factions are there - plus the enemies of whichever faction(s) you choose to ally with. Want to be a trader, making money in the shifting economy of space? There's tools for that, building up from one ship to a merchant fleet. Want to be a leader, forming your own power base to compete for the universe on your own? Can do, including building and outfitting your own fleet to defend space you've taken and attack for more.

But despite all of that, I can't recommend the game.

Because there's too many bugs. Go too fast at the wrong time, and you'll clip yourself into a building - and most of the recommendations of how to unclip involve getting out of your ship, into another ship, and leave the sector. Mission guidance usually works - but sometimes it fails, and I don't know why. For a few weeks, there was a bug involving Overwolf (which I use as a Minecraft launcher) that crashed the game. And then some times the game just quits - or worse, crashes my computer.

I've got 140+ hours on the game (which makes me relatively new, by some standards); but I don't remember the last time I've gotten to play for a full day (and the game is served by longer play sessions) without having to restart the game at least once - usually once every 2-3 hours. It's fine when I have the patience for that - but when I don't, it's not playable.

This review was written when I had ~40 hrs of play time, near the release of the game.  
  
This is a huge improvement over X Rebirth.  But there are still some problems.  

Ease of Access:  No manual and very little documentation.  The tutorials available from the help menu are difficult to follow and hang at certain steps sometimes not proceeding to the next stage of the tutorial.  A redesign of the tutorial system would be nice.  Having it as a popup or side window and allowing us to cycle back and forward between the stages in case we missed something or need to skip to a certain stage.  All in all, the lack of learning tools at this stage causes a huge learning curve.  There are all sorts of buttons and levers to press and you will have no idea what they do until you start pressing things.  And you won't have any idea which buttons you have to press to do something you want to do.  
  
Bugs/crashes:  I have encountered numerous bugs and a few crashes.  While most of the bugs I have encountered are not game breaking, they can be annoying.  Some of the bugs and crashes I have experienced are already patched and fixed.  I have had 2 hard crashes so far that have made my PC shutdown.  And a few crashes to desktop.  
  
Features:  As of writing this, the game doesnt seem to be feature complete.  Certain things have place holders but arent properly implemented.  That said, this game is so much better than X rebirth, and its closing the gap to being as rich an experience as X3.  I don't have any doubts that with a couple more years of work it will be way better than X3.  The foundation they have laid seems solid and robust.  Map and fleet controls are much easier now, but still need improvement, as some of the commands do not seem to work as intended yet.  Keymapping needs improvement.  The encylopedia seems to be missing a lot of information, hopefully they will expand the available info over time.  It's quite possible that I need to unlock that information myself with scanning and such?  

Would I recommend?  
Yes.  This is probably one of Egosofts best launches to date.  If you are a veteran to egosoft game launches, you know they launch a bit buggy and with some features not working as intended.  But they always patch them up and make the games better.  X4 is already a pretty awesome game and can only see it getting better with time.

This game is massive, and a short review would be a fib. X4 stacks systems inside systems and then invites you to live in the machine. My aim here is to put my experience into clear terms so prospective players know what they’re buying into, and so the developers can see where the edges still draw blood.

I can’t simply rubber-stamp “recommend / not recommend” because context does all the heavy lifting. X4 demands a serious time investment before the fun blooms. I started in the tutorials, took the hint toward an open start, and launched. The controls feel unfamiliar at first but settle into a logic that’s remarkably satisfying; the new flight model is superb, perhaps my favourite spaceship handling to date. Then the learning tax arrived. My first “clear a few pirates” job spiralled into faction-wide fury because I’d misunderstood a targeting option; I’d effectively told the universe that half the sector was hostile. That mistake is on me, but the tutorial UX doesn’t help: when a lesson offers multiple targeting modes, it hides the alternatives after a single choice, and it never clearly signals that you might have flipped a switch with big consequences. A small rethink—side-by-side options, a clear confirmation, an easy revert—would save a lot of new-player pain.

The same intent-vs-outcome problem shows up with friendly fire. If you deliberately hammer a friendly station, you deserve what’s coming. If you accidentally graze it with your main gun while defending it, the warning system is mostly fair. Where it breaks is turrets. They auto-engage, and in a dogfight near a friendly structure, stray hits can flip that structure hostile in seconds. There isn’t time to dig through behaviour menus mid-brawl, and switching turrets off often means getting swarmed. Subordinates can then escalate into a station fight you never wanted. A common defence is “in real life if you shoot, they shoot back,” which dodges the point: the game already infers intent in other places; it should do the same here. A simple grace model that distinguishes turret splash from aimed aggression, plus a context tag for “defending this asset” that lengthens forgiveness windows and lowers rep penalties, would keep the spirit of the system without punishing players for collateral they didn’t intentionally cause. A one-key “safe near friendlies” turret preset, and stricter rules to stop subordinates escalating against stations without explicit authorisation, would do wonders for sanity.

On performance and AI, there’s a trade-off people don’t like to acknowledge: if you want smarter behaviour, you’re asking the CPU to work harder. X4 is notoriously CPU-bound. On my machine—a Ryzen 9 9950X3D—the GPU often loafs while the CPU spikes; huge fleet actions can plunge to around 10 FPS, while free flight cruises at 100–140 FPS. The swings matter more than the peaks. I’d take steadier frame-times over headline highs any day. DLSS, in my case, muddies textures and offers only modest gains; clarity is more valuable in a sensor-heavy game than a few extra frames. If there’s one performance theme I’d love the devs to chase, it’s consistency: cap what you must, but keep big battles smooth enough to read and react. Adaptive AI tick rates and decision scopes based on battle size and player proximity could help trim the CPU spikes without gutting the simulation.

How does it feel once you’ve made your peace with the learning curve? Brilliant—and stubborn. X4 is the purest sci-fi sandbox around: build an empire, play lone wolf in a warship, mine, trade, follow the story, or simply wander. You can do all of it, often simultaneously. The friction comes not from what the game allows, but from how clearly it explains itself. I’m a min-maxer; I like to understand systems so I can plan. In X4, straightforward answers are frequently missing or inconsistent. The in-game encyclopaedia is thin, community resources are patchy or outdated, and terminology shifts between menus—“attack with commander” here, “attack” there—leaving you to guess the real scope of an order. Formations look nice, but what do they change? How should a fleet be structured for specific tasks? Too often you end up triangulating five contradictory forum posts and calling that knowledge.

Some players adore the mystery. I get the appeal. But if you want to broaden the audience and raise the ceiling on meaningful feedback, the game needs to communicate intent, not just keybinds. An official, versioned wiki that states plainly how orders resolve, what formations influence, how reputation and friendly-fire logic trigger, and which variables scale with what would be transformative. Consistent naming across every UI, with precise tooltips that explain scope (“wing executes target designated by commander”), would defog the command layer. An optional “Explain this” panel attached to each order—listing expected outcomes, prerequisites, and edge cases—plus a small sandbox scenario for testing formations, orders, and turret presets without consequences, would turn experimentation from guesswork into learning. An event log that says why something happened—rep drops, FF flags, subordinate escalations—would close the loop.

Praise where it’s due, because X4 earns it in style. Taking the helm of a battleship, jumping into a system, and watching your task force unfurl and get to work is joyous. The scale lands. The flight model sings. When it all clicks, it really clicks.

Verdict: X4 is a great game wrapped in sharp corners. It rewards patience, curiosity, and a strong CPU, and it stumbles on information design, inconsistent terminology, and friendly-fire edge cases that punish intent poorly. If you enjoy building machines and learning by tinkering, it delivers dozens—hundreds—of hours where the universe feels alive and responsive. If you prefer plug-and-play clarity, it will test your tolerance until the systems make sense.

I kept playing this game in a sunk cost fallacy hoping that at a certain stage it would get better, but it just.... it just never did.

1. The galaxy feels massive but ultimately vapid and hollow. The only thing big is space but that's a given and easy to accomplish. Things such as ships are disappointing because they feel so small. You can only visit the bridge and docking areas of any ship no matter how massive the ship is. Even the most volumetric carriers that takes hundreds of people to crew only has those two locations you can go to, both of which are very small. This is even worse on stations as no matter the size of the stations, you can only visit 3-4 tiny copy and pasted rooms minus the dock. You can't do something like go to a station that grows wheat and visit the wheat fields or go to an ore refinery and witness the factory chains that turn ore into metal.

2. NPCs are very awkward and stilted. NPCs pretty much do nothing except stand in place, either alone or in groups not talking to each other, and walk to and from the elevator. On ships they will "work" on terminals that you can't even interact with. They don't talk inherently outside of saying "hello" when you're near and in rare instances where they do talk, they talk like Oblivion NPCs. Space combat dialogue is literally just a bunch of trashtalking, like a gaming commercial's PG13 take on what a CoD lobby sounds like, and your crew is mute. It feels like it would benefit so much if your squad did stuff like notify you when they take down the engines of a capital ship or disarm it and if your onboard crew told you shields are low/down instead of the onboard AI and if turrets and stuff on your ship have been destroyed. I do love though how there are couches and stuff in the game, but you nor NPCs can actually physically sit in them. Very cool.

3. AI is atrociously pathetic in every regard. I lost a multi-million credit costing destroyer when I had my fleet siege an incomplete station that didn't even have weapons installed on it yet. The moment you start commanding multiple ships, the AI will begin to consistently give you a headache from that point onward. 
They seem to choose the worst ways to deal with situations, such as destroyers who have long range weapons for sieging charging directly into a station and dying in seconds. 
The AI can consistently get stuck doing most activities in the game it can do. 
The AI order priorities are also borked due to critical commands, which are commands that the AI WILL DO before doing anything else and what constitutes a critical command is not what you think they are. Things like attacking stuff is not a critical command. Instead, stuff like docking is. So if you have a carrier with ships and those ships after undocking are out of combat for .5 seconds, they will all redock at the carrier as a critical command, and if the carrier comes under attack again, the ships will do literally nothing until they redock and then immediately relaunch. The only critical command that works and makes sense is retreat, but that too is kinda borked because not giving combat vessels in combat new orders in a specific way will cause them to critically retreat. 
AI fleets also don't act like fleets, but rather just a group of units that are easier to select. Outside of formations, they don't work together and coordinate, especially ships assigned to carriers. I've lost ships in fleets because when I'm regrouping my ships in a fleet to attack an enemy fleet, some ships will just Leeroy Jenkins themselves right into the enemy fleet without the backup of the rest of their team. I've lost many many many credits due to the AI being reckless with my ships that I bought.
They can't even use combat ships effectively. The only thing they can use well are small ships. Medium ships are stuck in a catch-22 of being neither fast enough to avoid hits or tanky enough to take them, and as a result take far more casualties of their class than other ship sizes. Large ships are hard to aim for them, so they can't really hit any target with their main weapons other than stations. And as for carriers? No. Just no. Don't let the AI use a carrier, it's just borked. They'll be stuck for hours trying to redock their ships.

4. Management is a nightmare. There are a few systems in place to help make management easier, but there are neither enough and those that are there are poorly explained, if at all. The tutorials barely even get their toes wet with explaining all of this stuff. The in game tutorials are a bit better but are hands on, which is good for experience, but really bad if you only have a single question that needs to be answered and you need to replay the entire tutorial up to that point to get it answered. Management is still a pain, in the end, and could do with being more simplified and streamlined. Some mechanics are missing that I feel should be mandatory in games like this, such as the ability to quickly rebuild destroyed ships in a fleet, like Stellaris, instead of having to figure out what ships were lost in your large fleet, rebuilt all of those ships manually, wait for them to be built, command them to fly to the fleet, and then merge them into the appropriate groups. This gets really painful when managing fleets of over one hundred ships.

5. No character customization in a sandbox game with RPG elements. You can't even make a custom start, you can only choose a few preset starts with preset characters for each. A real shame, but given that that hasn't been pointed out by anyone else, maybe I'm the only one who cares about that sort of stuff.

6. The game progresses at a painfully slow pace. It feels like nothing happens unless you make it happen. It's like the world doesn't move on its own. Factions at war barely make progress in it, like a perpetual stalemate, except for the xenon who are honestly a non-issue and will just die out on their own eventually, with only one xenon sector actually making progress. If you feel the need to make a craftable fourth ship mode that speeds up time, you should probably rethink your approach to the game pacing. I loathe SETA because it is simultaneously the most effective way to make money and the least engaging way to do it. Just leave your computer on overnight and come back filthy stinking rich.

7. Factions are not really engaging. It doesn't really feel like you can join a faction, even if you "join" their war effort. You always feel like just a third party contracted for help as they give you tasks on some digital bulletin board. It would have been so much more engaging if you instead actually joined their armies and fought with them. Like if they planned to make a push into enemy territory, they would contact you and ask you to join them in X time and if you did, they would leave a spot open for your planned ship and then you could join their fleet and fly in formation with them using autopilot. But alas, that's not the case. You just feel like a mercenary for hire. And you can't even join fleets, only lead them.

I feel like I'm playing a beta game. Where all the core features are there, but are barely expanded on. It's like an ocean but it's all knee deep. If what you want to do is just jump into a fighter and pew pew the bad men, you would probably have fun here, because the game does nail the feeling of you just being a dude in a ship with big guns. But most things beyond that feel shallow, rarely make sense at a glance, and are tedious and finicky to work with. This game needs a lot of ironing out to be more playable and easy to manage and depth should not be neglected to make room for more width.

[u]Update[/u], 13.06.2026
Before I continue, there is one thing to keep in mind while reading this review: X4 was released in 2018. It is now 2026. The game has been on the market for eight years.

I decided to update my review because I have added another 400+ hours of gameplay since my original review. During that time I bought all DLCs except Timelines, because the reviews did not convince me, and the soundtrack DLCs. I played through Update 8.0 and also started a new game with Update 9.0.

Unfortunately, my recommendation remains the same: I still do not recommend the game.

Let's start with something basic: savegame names.

I do not know how other players manage their saves, but I like to name mine properly, for example "moving forward", "building a base", "before invasion", and so on. In almost every other game, once you name a save, the name stays there unless you change it. In X4, you have to type the name again and again. Every time.

This is a tiny thing, but it is exactly the kind of tiny thing that becomes ridiculous after eight years. It is basic usability.

Another example: autopilot and stopping the ship.

When I am on autopilot and press Backspace, which is my command to stop the engines, I expect the ship to stop. Instead, the ship can start spooling up travel drive again. Why? I gave the order to stop. There should be no interpretation needed here. Stop means stop.

Again: eight years.

Another example: taking command of your own ship.

You walk to the pilot seat, there is an NPC pilot sitting there, and the interaction says "Take command of ship". You click it. Why do I often need to click again to actually sit down and take control? Why is the first command not enough?

This is not a complex empire-management issue. This is basic interaction design.

Another example: combat rewards.

I can destroy a Xenon destroyer or even a Xenon defence station in faction space and most fo the time receive no  reward. Maybe this is because of proximity to faction stations, maybe it is some ownership or damage-credit issue, maybe there is another internal reason. The point is that from the player's perspective it simply feels inconsistent and unrewarding.

Now let's move to Update 9.0.

Autopilot appears to be worse than before. I have repeatedly seen the autopilot slow down, cancel travel acceleration, or fail to reach proper travel speeds for no obvious reason. Many other players have reported similar behaviour. In my case, I noticed it especially while flying the Hyperion. Since the Hyperion has a 60 km radar range, my suspicion is that the ship reacts more frequently to contacts appearing on radar, possibly because the improved combat AI or avoidance logic keeps recalculating something.

I may be wrong about the exact cause. Egosoft has the data and can verify that. But the practical result is what matters: autopilot now feels less reliable. If an "improvement" causes basic travel behaviour to become worse, then I have to question what exactly was improved.

And this is the recurring issue with X4.

The game keeps receiving updates, balance passes, new systems and new features, but many basic usability problems remain or getting worse. I am not even going to fully break down asset management, fleet management, order queues, formation flying, station management, or large-scale empire control here. That would require a separate review by itself.

But I will say this: X4 allows players to build very large industrial and military empires, while the tools for managing those empires still feel inadequate. At scale, the player often fights the interface more than the enemy.

This is the part I find most frustrating. The core idea of X4 is brilliant. The scale, the economy, the stations, the ships, the dynamic universe,all of that can be fascinating. But the game too often turns that potential into administrative friction.

If Egosoft eventually releases X5, I genuinely hope they do not treat it as just an opportunity for better graphics and more content. The fundamental user experience, command systems, asset management, and basic interaction logic need serious (re)work. Otherwise, players should expect the same problems again, only with a nicer coat of paint.

After more than 400 additional hours, my conclusion has not changed.

X4 is a fascinating game with enormous potential, but it is still buried under too many basic usability problems for me to recommend it.


[b]Original post[/b]
I really wanted to like X4: Foundations, because on paper this is exactly the kind of game I should love: start with one ship, build your way up, create trade networks, hire people, own stations, command fleets and eventually become a real force in the universe.

The problem is not the concept. The concept is excellent. The problem is that the game often feels like it actively fights against the player.

The early experience is especially bad. Instead of giving you a clear and satisfying first path into the sandbox, the game throws you into confusing objectives, poor guidance and missions that can be completely inappropriate for a new player. Being sent to locate and scan a Xenon base almost immediately is not "freedom", it is bad onboarding. A new player should not need to already understand half the game’s systems just to avoid wasting time or flying into a death trap.

Mission discovery is also terrible. You can sit at a major station, open mission offers and simply get nothing. No direction, no useful alternative, no clear explanation. The answer seems to be "fly around and maybe something appears." That is not depth. That is friction. A sandbox still needs a functional early-game loop. CGo wander around and hope the game starts" is not good design.

The user interface is another major problem. X4 often feels less like a space game and more like administrative software with spaceships attached. Basic things are needlessly awkward. Saving the game, renaming things, finding options, understanding what is happening on the map, figuring out what the game actually wants from you, too much of it feels clumsy, inconsistent or badly explained.

And this is the core issue: I want to play a game, not clock into a second job.

Complexity is not the problem. Factorio is complex. Good strategy games are complex. Deep simulations can be complex. But good complexity gives you tools, clarity and momentum. X4 too often gives you confusion, hidden rules and bad presentation, then expects the player to excuse it because the simulation underneath is ambitious.

There may be a great game buried here. I can believe that. I can believe that after tutorials, guides, YouTube videos, forum searches, mods and many hours of trial and error, X4 becomes impressive. But that is not a defense of the game. That is an admission that the game does a poor job of introducing and respecting the player.

Before buying DLC, players should seriously ask themselves whether they actually enjoy the base game’s systems, interface and pacing, or whether they are buying the fantasy of what X4 could be. More content does not fix a weak early experience, bad guidance or a UI that constantly gets in the way.

If you are already deeply invested in X4 and enjoy fighting through its systems, then maybe the DLC makes sense. But if you are a new player hoping for a smooth "start small and build an empire" space sandbox, be careful. The promise is fantastic. The execution can be exhausting.

For me, X4 is not bad because it lacks ambition. It is bad because it mistakes poor accessibility, weak onboarding and clumsy interface design for depth. A game can be deep without being hostile to basic enjoyment. X4 too often forgets that.

I own every game ever made by Egosoft. The concept of this game is fantastic. The cockpit experience is great. But the management mechanics are awful and the ability to command your own company (Ships and stations) is so frustrating that it almost seems intentionally designed to scare people off or make them just give up.

Example: I had a frigate protecting a miner that I was piloting, and bought a freighter to pick up extra mined ore. Well the freighter wouldn't pick up the ore. So I switched to the freighter, set the miner to automine, then the miner wouldn't mine anymore. That's just how it goes every single time you try to command other ships to do anything at all. You might be thinking 'but you assigned them to assist you, and you changed roles.' No, I reassigned everybody each time.

Pros;
- Great cockpit experience
- Nice ship variety
- Interesting weapons
- Lots to do
- Good stories if you care to find them
- Ability to build pretty much whatever you want, after you get some reputation

Cons
- The mechanics of ordering ships is god awful. Whomever designed it maybe shouldn't have anything to do with UX in the future.  Example. Want to assign a pilot to a ship? You don't just select the ship from the drop-down list-box. You then have to right click on that ship you already select and select 'Select Ship' Seriously?
- Infuriating lack of control over your subordinates
- Missing commands such as 'come pick me up in empty space,' ,etc.
- Commands that just don't work at all such as 'protect commander' and setting commander as your own ship.

[h1]It's a simulator.[/h1]

[u]New players to the X Series, start reading here.[/u]
If you're looking for a game with exciting dogfighting, you'll find better games for that with dogfighting being the core focus of its gameplay. The focus of this game is managing and directing supply chains, fleets, and factories. I've spend more time interfacing menus and hitting the fast-forward button, than actually flying around in various ships to shoot or trade stuff. The visuals, while nothing to boast about, is sorta the sprinkle on top. Everything in the game is to scale. 

Because of that, you really get to appreciate the vastness of the simulation. I can be standing on a station and order a large freighter that I own to stop making trade light years away, to land and pick me up, and then simultaneously watch it fly to the station on the map and out the window to see it flying in towards my position and dock right in front me. I can seamlessly then aboard and take control of the freighter (or stand in the cabin) and have the ship depart and fly towards a carrier ship hundreds of kilometers away. I can then land the freighter on to the carrier, and then fly the carrier to a waiting fleet of hundreds of ships.

At that point the framerate will slow down to a crawl because of the various calculations and renderings the computer is doing for my fleet and the enemy defences. I will lose hundreds of ships in the battle, but that's okay. Do you know why?

[b]It's because I spent hundreds of IRL hours starting out as a petty trader/miner/mercenary, then scraping enough to buy my first miner or freighter to automate trading/mining for me, to a point where I can buy more traders/miners so I can eventually generate enough income to build my first factory, then add on to the factory to make a janky complex with ineffecient supply-chain flow, then spending more time learning how to make more effecient/modular/scalable complexes to dominate the local market supply, so that I can finally begin to automate and on a whim build my own hundred-ship fleet using materials that I manufactured with my factory complexes. Did I mention that there's also a living and breathing economy in the game world?[/b]
